title: Introduction to Strings
description: Understand what strings are, how characters are stored, and basic string operations

blocks.text: So… what exactly is a string?
A string is a sequence of characters stored one after another in memory just like an array of characters. Each character sits at a specific index, starting at 0.
Take the word "hello":
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249614500-14430536.png
Each character is stored using a numeric code. In ASCII,
'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, 'z' = 122.
In modern languages, Unicode is used instead so that characters from any language on earth can be stored.
Just like arrays, you can access any character by index in O(1) time:

codes.python:
word = "python"

print(word[0])   # p
print(word[3])   # h
print(word[-1])  # n (last character)

blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
Here's a key difference from arrays in many languages, strings are immutable. That means once a string is created, you cannot change any character inside it directly.
In Python, if you try to do word[0] = 'J' on a string, you get an error. Instead, you have to build a new string.

Why does this matter?Every time you concatenate strings in a loop in Python or Java, a brand new string is created each time. Doing this n times costsO(n²)total. The fix is to collect parts in a list and join at the end — that's O(n).
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
1. Accessing a Character
Since a string is backed by a contiguous block of memory just like an array, any character can be read by index in O(1) time.
2. Traversal
Walking through every character one by one used for counting, searching, or transforming text. Visits each of the n characters once, so it's O(n).
3. Slicing / Substring
Extracting a portion of a string creates a brand new string it doesn't reuse the original memory. Slicing from index L to R copies (R − L) characters, so it costs O(n).

codes.python:
s = "abcdefgh"

print(s[2:6])  # cdef
print(s[0:3])  # abc
print(s[5:])   # fgh

blocks.text: 4. Concatenation
Joining two strings creates a new one in memory. A single concatenation of strings of length m and n takes O(m + n). Avoid doing this inside a loop use a list and join() instead.

codes.python:
result = ""
chars = ["d", "s", "a"]

for ch in chars:
    result += ch  # repeated concatenation

print(result)  # dsa

blocks.text: 5. Search / Pattern Matching

Checking whether a substring exists inside a string. The naive approach checks every starting position that's O(n × m) where n is the string length and m is the pattern length. Built-in methods like in or find() are optimised but still O(n × m) in the worst case.

codes.python:
s = "the quick brown fox"

print("fox" in s)        # True
print(s.find("quick"))  # 4
print(s.find("cat"))    # -1 (not found)

blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
String problems dominate coding interviews. Like arrays, they come down to recognising the right pattern.
1. Two Pointers
The same idea as with arrays one pointer at each end, moving inward. Especially powerful for palindrome checks and string reversal problems.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249616267-229119626.png
blocks.alt: Two pointers palindrome check: pointers at both ends of "level"

blocks.text: ↑ left matches right → move both inward
↑ left matches right → move both inward → pointers meet → palindrome!
This runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
2. Sliding Window
Used for problems that ask for the longest or shortest substring satisfying some condition. You expand the window to the right and shrink it from the left when the condition breaks.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249619201-295390454.png
blocks.alt: Sliding window "abc" with all unique characters

blocks.text: window = "abc" → all unique → expand
duplicate 'a' found → shrink from left → window = "bca"

blocks.text: 3. HashMap / Frequency Count
Many string problems come down to counting how often each character appears. A dictionary (hashmap) lets you store and look up character counts in O(1).
Common use cases include:

items: Check if two strings are anagrams
